result:
I'd like to write about lichens, because I think they're one of the more quietly radical things on the planet and almost nobody looks at them.

A lichen isn't an organism. It's a partnership—a fungus and an alga (sometimes a cyanobacterium, sometimes both) living so closely that they form a body neither could form alone. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and hands over sugar. For a long time biologists debated whether this was cooperation or a kind of controlled captivity, the fungus farming its algal cells. The honest answer seems to be: the question doesn't quite apply. The lichen is what happens when you stop asking who's in charge.

What gets me is how they treat time. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on Arctic rock that are probably several thousand years old—older than most human institutions, sitting there being pale green and unremarkable on a boulder. Geologists actually use them as clocks: measure the diameter of a lichen on a rockfall or a moraine and you can estimate when that surface was exposed. A thing so slow it becomes a measuring instrument for the landscape.

They also colonize what nothing else will touch. Bare basalt, gravestones, the aluminum siding of a gas station, the backs of beetles in some tropical forests. They were probably among the first living things to pull minerals out of raw rock and begin the long process of making soil. Which means the dirt everything else eventually grew in was, in part, lichen's doing—an act of patience so extended that it's easier to think of it as geology than biology.

And they're vulnerable in a specific way. Because they absorb water and nutrients straight from the air, with no roots to filter anything, they take in whatever the air carries. Sulfur dioxide kills many of them outright. So a city's lichens are a map of its pollution history: certain species vanished from London and Manchester during the industrial era and have been slowly creeping back over the last few decades as the air cleared. You can read the last two centuries of coal burning on the bark of an old oak, if you know what to look for.

I think I'm drawn to them because they resist the categories I'd reach for by default. Individual or collective? Neither, exactly. Fast or slow? Slow past the point where "slow" means anything. Alive? Obviously—but in a way that looks, from a human timescale, a lot like a stain. They're a reminder that most of what's going on in the world is happening at scales and in forms that don't announce themselves, and that "unremarkable" is usually a statement about the observer.

Next time you're near an old stone wall, put your face a few inches from it. There'll be something there, doing its thousand-year thing, entirely indifferent to whether you noticed.
